submission.natural_language_explanation: Retrospective lexical detector for one family of English relational word-forms: the vocabulary of opposition, bearing/direction, relative position and directed stance, strong on opposite, contrary, opposed/opposition, offense/offensive, defense/defensive, aggressive, hostile, combative, antagonistic, adversarial, positive, negative, plus, favourable, adverse, advantageous, detrimental, beneficial, advantage, front, ahead, forward, toward(s), approach, direction, oriented, incoming, outgoing, anterior, posterior, exterior, superior, prior, relative, comparative, inverse, complementary, perpendicular, adjacent, inclusive, exclusive, attention, attitude, response, initiative, strategy, warning, complaint, objection, behalf, liaison, letter and way (derived forms of a stem fire together, e.g. opposed/opposing/opposition and offense/offenses/offensive, while the bare verb 'oppose' is weak), and also on the bound pieces of the same vocabulary when BPE exposes them as their own token ('-ative' in talk-ative/figur-ative, '-versely' in in-versely, '-wards' in north-wards, '-clusive' in re-clusive). Membership is lexical rather than conceptual: everyday or process words for the same ideas are silent, including behind/back/left/right/top/bottom, war/fight/attack/battle/conflict/rival, dispute/debate/argument/controversy/confrontation, similar/equal/identical/related/relevant, difference/contrast/distinction, due/prone/liable/subject/capable, plan/view/opinion/position and angry/violent/proud/guilty, as are the connectives but/however/although/nevertheless and the negators not/never/no; the peak is on the word itself (74% of input attribution on it, and context shifts it by only about 0.3-0.6), while the negative pole is a near-constant 0.1-0.17 GELU-dip baseline with no token structure, i.e. feature-absent.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
On Tuesday evening the city council gathered in a chamber on the second floor to review next year's budget, a meeting that stretched past midnight and drew nearly two hundred residents into a room built for eighty. The finance director opened with a short summary of the shortfall: eleven million dollars, most of it from slower sales tax receipts and a settlement the city lost last spring after a long quarrel with the state over pension payments.

Road repairs dominated the first hour. Crews have patched the same stretches of Elm Street three times in two years, and the asphalt keeps cracking after every hard frost. A contractor explained that the base layer was never rebuilt, only covered, and that a proper job would cost about four times as much. Residents from the eastern district asked why their sidewalks remain unpaved while downtown gets new brick every other summer, and why the potholes on Vine are filled with gravel instead of asphalt.

The library board requested an extra two hundred thousand dollars to keep the branch on Cedar open on weekends. Usage has climbed steadily since the after-school program started, with children filling the reading room until closing. Several parents told the council that the branch is the only quiet place their kids can study, and that closing it would push them onto the street.

Parking fees took up the next hour. Store owners argued that higher meter rates would drive customers to the mall, while the transit office insisted the money is needed to fix the bus garage roof. A consultant presented a chart showing that turnover improves when prices rise, but nobody in the audience seemed convinced by the numbers, and one merchant waved a stack of receipts at the dais.

A proposal to convert the old rail depot into a grocery store drew cautious support. The developer promised forty jobs and a shuttle for seniors, though several neighbors worried about truck traffic on narrow streets and asked whether the loading bay could be moved to the alley. The planning office said it would need a traffic study first.

One exchange turned hostile near the end of the evening, when a resident accused the chair of ignoring the eastern district for a decade and of taking campaign money from the developer who owns the empty lot on Vine. The chair denied the charge, called the accusation unfair, and gaveled the session to a close shortly afterward.

The council will vote on the package at its next meeting, and the clerk will post the revised figures on the city website by Friday.
